title: Capillary Hemangioma: The 'Strawberry' Orbital Tumor
summary: The most common benign orbital tumor of childhood, characterized by a rapid proliferative phase followed by spontaneous involution. Mastery of its management is crucial to preventing permanent amblyopia.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Capillary hemangioma (Infantile Hemangioma) is a benign hamartomatous proliferation of vascular endothelial cells. It typically presents shortly after birth, undergoes rapid growth (proliferative phase), and slowly regresses over several years (involutional phase). Unlike vascular malformations, these are true neoplasms of the vascular endothelium and are GLUT-1 positive.

rows: Bright red 'strawberry' lesion; blanching with pressure
Bluish hue through skin; proptosis; mass effect
Associated with subglottic or hepatic lesions

content.explanation: S: Superficial (bright red), T: Three-to-one (F:M ratio), R: Rapid growth (first 6-12m), A: Astigmatism (main cause of vision loss), W: Watchful waiting (if no visual threat), B: Beta-blockers (Gold Standard), E: Endothelial (GLUT-1+), R: Regression (spontaneous by age 7-9), R: Red flags (proptosis/ulcer), Y: Young (neonatal presentation).

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapidly progressing proptosis with exposure keratopathy
Evidence of Optic Neuropathy (RAPD, disk edema)
Severe ulceration or secondary infection of the lesion
High-output heart failure (multiple systemic hemangiomas)
Subglottic hemangioma (stridor/respiratory distress)

sections.title: Natural History & Phases
content: Phase 1: Proliferation (0-12 months) - Rapid expansion; becomes 'angry' and bright red.
Phase 2: Early Involution (1-3 years) - Growth stops; color fades to a duller red/greyish-purple.
Phase 3: Late Involution (3-9 years) - Gradual replacement of vascular tissue with fibrofatty stroma.
Phase 4: Resolution (Age 7-10) - 75% show complete resolution; remaining may have telangiectasias or skin laxity.

sections.title: Management Strategy Algorithm
content: Step 1: Baseline Assessment - Measure vision, refraction (cylindrical error), and assess for ptosis.
Step 2: Risk Stratification - If no visual threat or ulceration -> Observation with serial photography.
Step 3: First-line Medical - Oral Propranolol (2-3 mg/kg/day). Monitor HR, BP, and Glucose.
Step 4: Topical Adjuncts - Timolol 0.5% gel forming solution for small superficial lesions.
Step 5: Second-line - Intralesional Triamcinolone/Betamethasone (risk of CRAO) or systemic steroids.
Step 6: Surgical Intervention - Reserved for refractory cases, severe ptosis, or failed medical therapy.

sections.title: Medical Therapy: The Propranolol Revolution
content: Dosage: 2 to 3 mg/kg/day, typically divided into BID or TID dosing.
Mechanism: Vasoconstriction, inhibition of angiogenesis (VEGF), and induction of apoptosis.
Contraindications: Asthma, Bradycardia, Heart Block, Hypoglycemia.
Monitoring: Check BP and HR 1-hour post-first dose; advise parents on 'feed before dose' to avoid hypoglycemia.
Duration: Usually continued until 12-18 months of age to prevent rebound growth.

sections.title: Surgical Indications & Techniques
content: Indications: Amblyopia non-responsive to occlusion, severe exposure keratopathy, or psychosocial distress.
Pre-op: Consider embolization for massive high-flow lesions.
Approach: Anterior orbitotomy for pre-septal or localized orbital lesions.
Complications: Significant intraoperative hemorrhage is common; use meticulous hemostasis/cautery.
Laser: Pulsed-dye laser (585nm) for very thin superficial skin components.

sections.title: Vision-Threatening Complications
content: Amblyopia: Anisometropic (due to astigmatism) or Deprivational (due to ptosis).
Optic Nerve Compression: Rare but leads to irreversible optic atrophy.
Strabismus: Mechanical restriction of extraocular muscles.
Exposure Keratopathy: Due to extreme proptosis or lagophthalmos.
Intralesional Steroid Risk: Retrograde injection into CRAO (central retinal artery occlusion).

sections.title: Pediatric & Systemic Pearls
content: PHACE Syndrome: Posterior fossa malformations, Hemangioma, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac/Coarctation, Eye anomalies.
Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome: Consumptive coagulopathy (more common in Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma).
Refraction: Perform cycloplegic refraction every 3 months during the proliferative phase.
Amblyopia: Treat aggressively with patching if anisometropia >1.50D exists.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence: Léauté-Labrèze et al.
sections.content: The accidental discovery of Propranolol's efficacy in 2008 by Dr. Léauté-Labrèze transformed the field. Subsequent RCTs confirmed it as superior to steroids in both efficacy and safety. The 2015 NEJM trial demonstrated a 88% success rate with oral propranolol at 3mg/kg/day for 6 months compared to 4% for placebo.
